briefing: Zelenskyy says Ukraine is done pausing drone strikes on Russian oil refineries because Russia kept hitting Ukraine's power grid, and an Iranian naval commander now claims the Strait of Hormuz is closed after two ships sank there. Brent crude eased to about $104 in early trading on reports Washington may loosen some shipping sanctions, but fuel prices are likely to stay high. At home, Carney rallies in Calgary tonight ahead of Monday's Alberta referendum, and Bloor West bike lane removal continues in Toronto.
headline: Ukraine resumes refinery strikes; Iran claims Hormuz is closed

keyDates.label: Alberta vote; CPI; Commons returns
keyDates.why: Albertans vote on separation and other questions, Statistics Canada releases September inflation, and MPs return to Ottawa.

keyDates.label: B.C. provincial election
keyDates.why: British Columbians vote in Premier David Eby's snap election; advance voting runs October 16–21.

keyDates.label: Ontario municipal elections
keyDates.why: Toronto, Mississauga, Markham and every other Ontario city elect mayors, councillors and school trustees; Toronto polls open 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

keyDates.label: Israeli election; Queen's Park returns
keyDates.why: Israel votes amid talk of another strike on Iran, and Ontario's legislature sits again after a 21-week break.

keyDates.label: Bank of Canada decision
keyDates.why: Rate call and new economic forecast after two straight months of job losses.

keyDates.label: U.S. midterm elections
keyDates.why: Control of Congress decides how much room Trump has on tariffs and the Iran war.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, 2026, in the middle of nuclear talks. The first wave killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran answered with missiles and drones on Israel, Gulf states and U.S. bases, and closed the Strait of Hormuz, the channel that roughly a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through. A peace memorandum signed in June briefly reopened shipping, but it fell apart in July when Iran started attacking commercial ships again to press its claim over the strait.
stories.headline: Iran claims Hormuz is closed after two cargo ships sink
stories.impact: This is a big part of why gas and diesel in Ontario stay expensive, and diesel feeds straight into grocery and delivery prices. Higher fuel also pushed Canadian inflation up earlier this year, which is one reason the Bank of Canada has been cautious about cutting rates.
stories.now: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says GFS Pride hit a naval mine while using an unauthorized route, but a U.S. official says Iran attacked the ship, likely with a missile, and maritime security firm Marisks found no independent evidence of a mine. All 21 crew of GFS Pride got off safely; its sister ship GFS Giselle was hit too but reached anchorage. Admiral Habibollah Sayyari claimed Thursday that Iran has full control over the strait, and Reuters sources say Tehran is changing tactics to keep oil prices high before the U.S. midterms. The UK's maritime security agency has logged about 20 attacks in the strait since October 1. Oil eased Thursday morning on reports the U.S. is considering relaxing sanctions on some tankers, while Trump says the U.S. will not attack Iran before the November 3 midterms.

stories.summary: An Iranian naval commander says the Strait of Hormuz is closed and any ship passing through must coordinate with Iran, a day after the container ship GFS Pride and the bulk carrier Cape Dao sank nearby. Brent crude slipped about 1.5% to roughly $104 a barrel in early Thursday trading.

timeline.event: Hezbollah joins; Israel invades southern Lebanon. Houthis enter the war.
Two-week ceasefire; talks in Islamabad fail and the U.S. blockades Iran.
Islamabad Memorandum signed; both blockades lifted.
Ceasefire collapses after Iran attacks ships in Hormuz.
GFS Pride and Cape Dao sink; Brent settles at $106.
Iranian commander claims strait is closed; Brent dips to ~$104.

stories.why: This is the single biggest driver of global energy prices this year. Sinkings are rare, so two in a day signal Iran is willing to raise the stakes for all cargo, not just oil tankers, which can push up shipping and insurance costs.

stories.backstory: The U.S. Supreme Court struck down Trump's broad emergency tariffs in February, but sector tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos, copper and lumber stayed. At the first CUSMA review on July 1, the U.S. refused to extend the deal for a full new term, so it now needs annual reviews. Ottawa walked out of talks on August 21, calling Washington's last-minute demands unfair. The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on August 22, and Canada matched with counter-tariffs on September 8, plus a $25B support package for affected workers and businesses.
stories.headline: U.S. ambassador warns Canadian politicians off the midterms as Poilievre tours Michigan
stories.impact: Tariffs raise prices on some U.S. goods in Canadian stores and squeeze manufacturing jobs in the GTA, Windsor and Hamilton. If you or your family work in autos, steel, logistics or anything that ships to the U.S., this is the story most likely to touch your paycheque.
stories.now: On a podcast, Hoekstra pointed to Industry Minister Mélanie Joly's talk of aiming counter-tariffs at politically sensitive U.S. states and to Ontario's 2025 Reagan anti-tariff ad as examples that could look like interference. He did not name Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, who this week met auto and electrical workers in Detroit and Dearborn to argue for tariff-free auto trade. Poilievre says the visit is not meddling; White House trade adviser Peter Navarro had earlier warned Canada would pay a price. In Michigan, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers now calls the tariffs too high.

sources.title: CP24 (Canadian Press): Hoekstra warns Canadian politicians
CP24 (Canadian Press): Poilievre visits Detroit

stories.summary: U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra said Washington is watching for Canadian interference in the midterms and will respond if it sees any. Trump has threatened to raise the 25% U.S. tariff on Canadian autos to 50% on January 1.

timeline.event: U.S. adds lumber, furniture and cabinet tariffs.
U.S. Supreme Court strikes down emergency (IEEPA) tariffs.
CUSMA review: U.S. won't extend; annual reviews begin.
Canada exits talks; U.S. 50% tariffs take effect.
Canada's counter-tariffs on ~C$27.6B of U.S. goods.
Poilievre in Detroit; Trump eyes 50% auto tariff Jan 1.
Ambassador Hoekstra warns against midterm interference.

stories.why: About three-quarters of Canada's exports normally go to the U.S. Ontario, with its auto plants and steel mills, is the most exposed province.

stories.backstory: Russia's full-scale invasion is in its fifth year. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have been trying to coax Moscow back to talks, and reportedly see letting Russian diesel back onto the market as a carrot. European intelligence services warn Russia may take bigger risks against NATO countries in the coming months.
stories.headline: Zelenskyy ends pause on strikes against Russian oil refineries
stories.impact: Ukrainian hits on Russian refineries can tighten world diesel supply, which matters because diesel already feeds grocery and delivery costs in Ontario. Canada is a NATO member and a major Ukraine backer, so a widening split between Washington and Kyiv affects Ottawa's defence and aid decisions.
stories.now: The pause had been a response to a U.S. request after Trump announced an energy ceasefire on October 11, which Kyiv says it was not told about in advance. Overnight Russian attacks killed three people in Kropyvnytskyi and two in Dnipropetrovsk region, after Tuesday's barrage of 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones left about 600,000 people without power and hit all three of Kyiv's combined heat and power plants. Starlink access for Ukraine's drones was throttled without warning this week; Elon Musk says only the U.S. president decides limits on the military system. Ukraine's security service (SBU) says it stopped an 18-year-old suspected Russian agent from activating 148 Starlink terminals for Russian forces.

sources.title: Kyiv Independent: Zelensky lifts pause on refinery strikes
CP24 (AP): Russia keeps striking Ukraine's energy sites

stories.summary: Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that Ukraine is lifting its three-day pause on drone strikes against Russian refineries because Russia kept attacking Ukraine's power grid. He says Kyiv would only stop again in exchange for more U.S. Patriot air-defence missiles.

timeline.event: An earlier Trump-announced energy truce fails to take hold.
Trump announces an energy ceasefire; Ukraine pauses refinery strikes.
Zelenskyy says U.S. warned it could cut intelligence sharing.
Massive strike on Kyiv power plants; Starlink slowdown.
Zelenskyy lifts the pause on refinery strikes.

stories.why: Refinery strikes are Ukraine's main way to squeeze Russia's oil income, and dropping the pause puts Kyiv openly at odds with Trump's ceasefire push. With winter coming and Ukraine's grid badly damaged, the fight over energy targets could shape the next phase of the war.

stories.backstory: Canada's economy has been weak all year, squeezed by U.S. tariffs and by fuel-driven inflation from the Iran war. The Bank of Canada held its key rate at 2.25% through the summer and forecast just 0.7% growth for 2026.
stories.headline: Canada sheds 68,000 jobs in September, erasing this year's gains
stories.impact: If you're job hunting, especially as a student or new grad, the market is tougher right now. On the flip side, a rate cut would lower variable mortgage and line-of-credit payments.
stories.now: Statistics Canada says employment fell 68,000 in September after a 42,000 drop in August. Education lost the most jobs (35,000), followed by health care and manufacturing. Ontario lost 20,000 jobs in the month, though it is still up about 86,000 from a year ago. Youth employment dropped by 48,000.

sources.title: Statistics Canada: Labour Force Survey, September 2026
CBC: Canada lost 68,000 jobs in September

stories.summary: Unemployment rose to 6.5% after a second straight month of losses. Ontario's rate is 7.0%, and youth unemployment sits at 13%.

timeline.event: Inflation rises to 3.2%, driven by gasoline.
Bank of Canada holds at 2.25%, sixth straight hold.
Canada loses 42,000 jobs.
Another 68,000 jobs lost; unemployment 6.5%.

stories.why: Two bad months in a row raise the odds the Bank of Canada cuts rates on October 28, and they hint that the economy may be sliding toward recession.

stories.backstory: Premier Danielle Smith announced the referendum in February and added the separation question in May. A yes on that question would not take Alberta out of Canada; it would start a process toward a later, binding referendum. Other questions ask about provincial control over immigration, proof of citizenship to vote, and making provincial law override federal law.
stories.headline: Carney rallies in Calgary Thursday as Smith says she voted to stay
stories.impact: Indirect for Ontario, but a strong separatist showing would dominate federal politics and could affect transfer payments and national programs that every province shares.
stories.now: Elections Alberta counted 174,532 ballots on the first day of advance voting Tuesday, and heavy lines kept some polls open late. Carney's Calgary schedule Thursday includes meetings with community members, union workers and students before the 6:45 p.m. rally, organized by the campaign led by former deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk. Some critics question whether Ottawa has a strong enough ground game. Advance voting runs to Saturday, and voting day is Monday, October 19. Elections Alberta calls the separation question non-binding.

sources.title: CTV News (CP): Smith casts vote to stay in Canada
CTV News: 174,500 vote on first day of advance polls
Prime Minister's Office: Itinerary for October 15
The Hub: Carney urges Albertans to reject separation

stories.summary: Premier Danielle Smith says she voted at an advance poll for Alberta to remain in Canada while urging support for the other nine questions. Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks at a 'Forever Canadian' rally in Calgary Thursday evening and in Edmonton Friday.

timeline.event: Smith announces a fall referendum.
Separation question added to the ballot.
Léger poll: 70% stay, 22% start separation process.
Advance voting opens with 174,532 ballots on day one; Smith votes to stay.

stories.why: Even a non-binding result shapes national politics, federal-provincial relations and investor confidence in the energy sector.

stories.backstory: Premier Doug Ford's government passed a 2024 law letting it remove bike lanes on major Toronto roads, arguing they worsen traffic. A lower court ruled in 2025 that the law violated the Charter, but in August a three-judge appeal panel unanimously reversed that.
stories.headline: Crews start removing Bloor West bike lanes; one arrest at protest
stories.impact: Expect lane restrictions and protests on Bloor West between Royal York and Islington through mid-November, whether you drive, bike or take the bus there. How much this costs is also a live question in the October 26 mayoral vote.
stories.now: The work covers about a kilometre of Bloor between Royal York Road and Islington Avenue, and the city's notice says it should run until November 17. Ontario plans to rework up to 19 km of Toronto's protected bike lanes; the city estimates removing the Bloor, Yonge and University lanes would cost $48 million, a figure the province disputes. Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria says a design keeping one bike lane between Kipling and Islington would cost $750,000, while a provincially commissioned engineering report found the traffic benefits would be small or short-lived. Mayor Olivia Chow calls the plan a waste of money; challenger Brad Bradford supports removing these lanes. Cycle Toronto expects protests to continue and is asking the Supreme Court of Canada to hear its case.

sources.title: CP24: 1 arrested as cyclists try to block removals
National Observer: Crews remove bike lanes as protesters rally
CBC: Cyclist protest blocks removal start

stories.summary: Provincial crews returned in daylight Wednesday and began removing bike lanes on Bloor Street West in Etobicoke while police kept protesters back. A 25-year-old Hamilton man was charged with mischief and obstructing police.

timeline.event: Ontario passes law allowing bike lane removal.
Lower court blocks removal under the Charter.
Court of Appeal lets removal proceed.
Protest stalls first night of work; Supreme Court appeal sought.
Daytime removal begins; one arrest.

stories.why: It's the sharpest clash between Queen's Park and Toronto city hall, landing right before the municipal vote.

stories.backstory: Chow won a 2023 by-election after John Tory resigned and is now seeking a full term. Bradford, a councillor, is her main challenger. Late-summer polls had Chow around 50% and Bradford near 39%. Big themes are housing costs, traffic, property taxes and the province's moves on bike lanes.
stories.headline: New poll shows Toronto mayor's race tightening two weeks before the vote
stories.impact: You get a vote for mayor, ward councillor and school trustee in your own city. Check your municipality's site for your polling station and advance-voting hours.
stories.now: Sunday, October 11, set a single-day advance-voting record of 53,363 ballots, beating the 2023 by-election record of 38,621. Nanos surveyed 757 Torontonians October 8–10 (margin of error ±3.6 points); 17% of all respondents are still undecided. Chow leads strongly in Toronto and East York, Bradford leads in North York and Etobicoke, and Scarborough is roughly tied. Election day is Monday, October 26, with Toronto polls open 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.; Mississauga, Markham and the rest of the GTA vote the same day.

sources.title: CP24: Advance voting nearly doubles
CP24: Chow's lead shrinks in new poll
City of Toronto: Elections

stories.summary: A record 225,550 Torontonians voted in advance polls, nearly double the 2022 total. A Nanos poll puts Olivia Chow at 51% and Brad Bradford at 47% among decided voters, down from a lead of nearly 10 points.

timeline.event: Chow wins Toronto mayoral by-election.
Chow and Bradford register to run.
Polls show Chow ahead by 7–15 points.
225,550 vote early; Nanos poll shows a 4-point race.
Voting day across Ontario.

stories.why: City councils set property taxes, transit service, policing budgets and local housing approvals, and they last four years.

stories.backstory: The Houthis, an Iran-aligned movement controlling much of northern Yemen, joined the Iran war in late March by firing at Israel. Since then the fight has widened into a direct Saudi-Houthi confrontation, with Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and on the East-West oil pipeline that Saudi Arabia uses to bypass Hormuz.
stories.headline: Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh airport and Aramco sites, vow more
stories.impact: Indirect but real: more disruption to Red Sea shipping means slower and pricier imported goods and another push on fuel prices in Canada.
stories.now: The Houthis say the attacks answer Saudi threats against Sanaa and promise more strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities, telling workers and civilians to stay away. Riyadh's airport has been suspended through October 17, and U.S. government staff now need special permission to use any Saudi airport. The UN World Food Programme says the fighting is cutting off food aid to about 800,000 Yemenis, and the WHO says suspected cholera cases tripled in three weeks. Trump says he would consider joining Saudi strikes but only after the midterms.

sources.title: Middle East Monitor: Houthis renew attacks on Riyadh airport, Aramco
CBS News: Iran war live updates
Gulf News/AFP: Aramco building fire, 4 hurt in Riyadh

stories.summary: Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claims a ballistic missile hit Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and that missiles and drones struck Aramco sites in Dhahran and a refinery in Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the claims; the coalition says it intercepted a missile aimed at the capital Wednesday.

timeline.event: Houthis enter the Iran war with launches at Israel.
Houthi attack briefly shuts Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline.
Repeated attacks close Riyadh's airport; 20+ killed in a week.
Missile hits Aramco's Dhahran complex; 4 hurt by debris in Riyadh.
New missiles at Riyadh; Houthis claim airport and Aramco hits.

stories.why: If the U.S. joins, the war gains another front, and the Red Sea route through Bab el-Mandeb could become as dangerous as Hormuz. That would hit the backup routes the world is relying on for oil and container shipping.

stories.backstory: Cleveland-Cliffs bought Stelco in 2024. Ottawa approved the deal under the Investment Canada Act on the condition that it keep union jobs and most non-union positions, more than 1,500 in total.
stories.headline: NDP leaders urge Ottawa to nationalize Stelco as Hamilton layoffs roll out
stories.impact: Steel layoffs ripple through suppliers and local businesses across the Golden Horseshoe. It also signals how hard Ottawa will push on other foreign-owned plants in Ontario.
stories.now: Layoffs are rolling out over about three weeks; the steelworkers' local expects 300 to 350 in Hamilton, with more at Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke. Lewis argues a lawsuit would be too slow and points to Britain's nationalization of British Steel in July; the Ontario NDP also wants provincial tariff relief and Buy Ontario rules. Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves says the cuts are temporary, that the deal doesn't guarantee day-to-day staffing, and that he's ready to fight in court and open to selling. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says the 2024 takeover conditions are binding, and a court could order compliance, penalties or a sale.

sources.title: SMM: NDP leaders call to nationalize Stelco
CBC: Cliffs CEO prepared to fight Canada in court
Global News: Joly presses Stelco for job plan

stories.summary: Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis and Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles want Ottawa to take over Stelco after its U.S. owner, Cleveland-Cliffs, refused to halt layoffs. Ottawa is threatening court action instead.

timeline.event: Ottawa approves Cleveland-Cliffs' purchase of Stelco with job conditions.
Stelco says up to 500 Hamilton jobs will go.
Joly demands a plan within five business days.
Cliffs CEO says he'll fight in court; layoffs under way.
Federal and Ontario NDP call for nationalization.

stories.why: It's a test of whether Canada can enforce promises foreign buyers make, and a sign of how the trade war is landing on Ontario steel towns.

stories.backstory: Police identified a suspect vehicle and arrested two people within a day of the July abduction, and the investigation grew from there. Toronto police say crimes targeting people's digital assets are becoming more sophisticated and targeted. Military police are now running their own investigation alongside Toronto police. None of the charges has been tested in court.
stories.headline: Three military reservists among seven charged in Toronto crypto kidnapping
stories.impact: If you hold cryptocurrency, be careful about who knows it and how much you share online. The case may also lead to tighter controls at reserve armouries like Moss Park downtown.
stories.now: Police say a man was grabbed on July 25 as he approached his car, handcuffed and assaulted while his captors tried to get into his cryptocurrency and business security systems, then released and warned not to go to police. Charges include kidnapping for ransom, forcible confinement and gun and drug trafficking offences. Two of the soldiers, Bombardiers Talarambage Fernando, 22, and James Moreau, 29, belong to the 7th Toronto Regiment, a reserve artillery unit at Moss Park Armoury, and have been removed from duty. Police also seized guns with 3D-printed parts, GPS trackers and large amounts of methamphetamine and cocaine. The military had not reported the ammunition as stolen; the Department of National Defence says it is tightening ammunition tracking.

sources.title: CP24: 3 CAF members charged in abduction probe
CBC: 3rd CAF member charged in Toronto kidnapping
Global News: Military ammo recovered in kidnapping probe

stories.summary: Toronto police laid 82 charges against seven people, three of them Canadian Armed Forces members, after a July abduction near Finch and Bayview. About 2,500 rounds of ammunition stolen from the military were recovered.

timeline.event: Man abducted near Finch and Bayview; released hours later.
Police identify a vehicle and arrest two suspects.
Seven charged, including three CAF members; stolen ammo recovered.

stories.why: It raises questions about how the military keeps track of weapons and ammunition at reserve units, and it is a warning that people known to hold crypto can be targeted in person.

stories.backstory: Career colleges are private schools offering short job-training programs, and their students can get provincial grants and loans through OSAP. In February, the sector's own association flagged 14 campuses for possible suspicious activity. A May order cut six schools off from OSAP for 2026–27, and most are fighting it in court. In August the province brought in the auditing firm KPMG and referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police.
stories.headline: Ontario bars three GTA career college campuses from OSAP until 2029
stories.impact: If you or someone in your family is enrolled at a career college, check whether your OSAP funding is affected and talk to the school about options. For taxpayers, it's a test of whether the province can recover or stop misused student aid.
stories.now: The ministry says inspections found courses sometimes completed in a single day and students who could not name their school or program; these are allegations and have not been tested in court. The schools call the decision unreasonable and unfair, say students may have ignored verification calls thinking they were scams, and say they have added monitoring. The Bay Street campus grew from 996 OSAP students in 2021–22 to 7,435 in 2024–25, receiving over $108 million in grants that year, and the Brampton East campus received over $64 million. OSAP payments to career colleges and private schools are paused while an audit continues.

sources.title: CP24 (Canadian Press): Ontario blocks career colleges from OSAP

stories.summary: Colleges Minister Nolan Quinn has blocked three Academy of Learning locations from the Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) until at least the 2029–30 school year. Inspectors allege some coursework may have been done by third parties.

timeline.event: 14 campuses flagged for suspicious activity.
Six schools barred from OSAP for 2026–27.
KPMG audit; matter referred to OPP.
Three Academy of Learning sites barred to 2029–30.

stories.why: The three campuses alone took roughly a fifth of the nearly $1 billion in OSAP grants paid to career-college students in 2024–25, so the case is about how a large pot of public money was spent.
